newsitem.title: CHINA: China orders crackdown on illegal explosives.
newsitem.headline: China orders crackdown on illegal explosives.

text.p: China on Thursday ordered a police crackdown on the production of illegal explosives, two days after three time-bombs exploded in the restive Moslem region of Xinjiang in the country's far west.

A circular from the Ministry of Public Security, printed in the official People's Daily newspaper, said illegal explosives were flooding the country and that some were being used by "criminal elements" to destabilise society.

Police should spare no efforts to track down illegal production of explosives and monitor the use of materials used to make them, the circular said, adding that those found contravening Beijing's explosives laws should be pursued and punished.

It called on police to cooperate with local government and Communist Party leaders to tighten supervision, particularly in rural areas where home-made explosives are often produced for use in small mines and quarries and frequently cause accidents.
The circular said that in many regions the production, sale, warehousing, transport and use of explosive materials "show serious problems of chaotic management".
"This has caused a great flood of explosives into society, with some being used by criminal elements to commit acts that cause great harm to social stability and public safety," the circular said.
The directive came two days after three time-bombs exploded in Urumqi, the centre of Chinese control over Xinjiang and its ethnic Uighur population.

The explosions, which killed at least four people and injured about 60, occurred as the final rites were being observed in far-off Beijing for Deng Xiaoping, the paramount leader who strictly enforced the integrity of China against separatist threats.

Despite widespread fear of further unrest, state media have not reported the incidents, the first known violence in Xinjiang -- a region that Moslem separatists call East Turkestan -- since anti-Chinese riots in Yining on February 5 and 6 left nine people dead.

No one has claimed responsibility for Tuesday's blasts. Xinjiang, bordering Afghanistan, Pakistan and three mostly Moslem Central Asian states, was shaken last year by attacks on officials and Moslem leaders regarded as pro-Beijing.
